report:
The evidence is more nuanced than a simple "no." The research is genuinely mixed, with the debate centering on whether observed associations reflect true causation or **confounding by indication** (i.e., benzodiazepines are prescribed for anxiety, insomnia, and depression — which can themselves be early/prodromal symptoms of dementia).

**Studies finding an increased risk:**
- A 2014 case-control study found that past benzodiazepine use was associated with a 43–51% increased risk of Alzheimer's, with a dose-response pattern (84% higher risk for those taking higher cumulative doses) ([Joyce 2022, Alzheimer's & Dementia](https://alz-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/trc2.12309); [Harvard Health Blog](https://www.health.harvard.edu/blog/benzodiazepine-use-may-raise-risk-alzheimers-disease-201409107397)).
- A meta-analysis found heavy cumulative benzodiazepine doses were associated with increased dementia risk ([Alz Discovery](https://www.alzdiscovery.org/cognitive-vitality/blog/do-benzodiazepines-pose-a-dementia-risk-yes-no-maybe)).
- Z-drugs like zolpidem have also shown associations with dementia in some studies ([ExcelMale summary](https://www.excelmale.com/threads/does-zolpidem-ambien-increase-dementia-risk-what-the-research-actually-shows.34592/)).

**Studies finding no causal link:**
- A large nationwide cohort and nested case-control study published in the *American Journal of Psychiatry* found that benzodiazepines and Z-drugs did **not** increase subsequent dementia risk once confounding was addressed ([Healio](https://www.healio.com/news/psychiatry/20200414/benzodiazepines-zdrugs-do-not-increase-dementia-risk)).
- A systematic review found the association with benzodiazepines "did not persist after exclusion of studies with potential reverse causation and confounding by indication" ([Dundee discovery](https://discovery.dundee.ac.uk/en/publications/use-of-sedative-hypnotic-medications-and-risk-of-dementia-a-syste/)).
- A 2020 editorial in *Psychiatry Online* concluded that benzodiazepine use does not cause dementia ([Psychiatry Online](https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/appi.ajp.2020.20040375)).

**Bottom line:** The answer leans toward "no" in the sense that the best-designed studies (which account for reverse causation) do not support a causal link. However, long-term benzodiazepine use is still associated with cognitive impairment and other serious risks in older adults, so caution in prescribing remains warranted.
